articles.title: Alex Pretti’s family calls for accountability 7 months after fatal CBP shooting
articles.summary: The family of Alex Pretti, the ICU nurse who was fatally shot by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents during a January crackdown on immigration in Minnesota, called for answers from the Trump administration on Tuesday — seven months after his death. “I was not shocked that he helped somebody. My shock is that he…
articles.body:
The family of Alex Pretti, the ICU nurse who was fatally shot by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents during a January crackdown on immigration in Minnesota, called for answers from the Trump administration on Tuesday — seven months after his death.

“I was not shocked that he helped somebody. My shock is that he was murdered and no one has given us the complete truth or anyone has been held accountable,” his mother, Susan Pretti, told ABC News ‘ George Stephanopoulos during a “Good Morning America” interview. “And it’s been seven months.”

Witnesses of the shooting said they saw the slain nurse recording immigration officers with his cellphone while trying to help up a woman who one agent had pushed down. Law enforcement officials then surrounded the 37-year-old, with one appearing to wrestle Pretti’s firearm — for which he had a permit — away before two agents fired several shots at him.

The Hennepin County Medical Examiner ruled his death a homicide . But, while the two officers were charged for use of force, they have not been charged for the killing.

Susan Pretti, sat alongside her husband Michael Pretti and daughter Micayla Pretti, added that there was “more effort in vilifying him than pursuing justice, investigating this.”

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem accused Alex Pretti of being involved in an “act of domestic terrorism” for endangering the agents’ lives, mimicking her description of Renee Good — a Minneapolis resident killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers earlier the same month.

Other Trump administration officials, including White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, called Alex Pretti a “domestic terrorist” and an “assassin.” President Trump himself wrote on Truth Social that ICU nurse was “perhaps” an “insurrectionist.”

“It’s so un-presidential,” Michael Pretti said. “It’s ridiculous that, you know, the leader of the free world speaks that way about an American citizen.”

His father added that their son cared about his community and was only observing immigration officials’ activity in Minneapolis, not protesting against them.

“We’ve seen what happened,” Michael Pretti noted. “The videos are pretty clear. But we want justice. We want accountability for the people that did this to Alex.”

The family learned about his death while watching news coverage of immigration enforcement in the city, seeing footage of “our son be shot 10 times on TV,” the father said.

“What did he do to deserve to be murdered?” Susan Pretti asked. “To be left cold, on the ground, dead, my child? What did he do?”

She asked why the family “should not get” an apology.

Steve Schleicher, an attorney for the Pretti family, told ABC News that the family deserves to know who shot their son and that that person or persons should be prosecuted.

The Department of Justice opened a civil rights investigation into the shooting shortly after Alex Pretti’s death, pledging to work in tandem with the FBI and a division of the Department of Homeland Security.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, then serving as deputy attorney general, said prior to announcing the probe that Alex Pretti’s actions did not match “the legal definition of domestic terrorism.” After the announcement, Blanche added that he was “not committing to anything with respect to that investigation.”

Last month, Minnesota officials obtained body camera footage and other evidence from the federal government of the shootings of both Alex Pretti and Good. The FBI had previously said it would not share evidence related to Alex Pretti’s death with Minnesota investigators.

“My aim has always been to ensure justice is done, and this evidence-sharing is a positive development in that essential work,” Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said after obtaining the footage.

articles.title: Democratic newcomer scores runoff upset in Oklahoma, vows to impeach Trump if elected
articles.summary: N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas defeated Jim Priest in the runoff race for the Democratic Senate nomination in Oklahoma.
articles.body: A political newcomer just scored a victory in ruby-red Oklahoma, and, if elected, she would put all her energy into impeaching President Donald Trump. N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, a nurse who has never run for office before, bested Jim Priest, a lawyer and nonprofit executive, in the runoff race for the Democratic Senate nomination in Oklahoma. Thomas, though a new face, scored the highest percentage of votes in the June primary contest that featured five total candidates vying for the nomination. It tees up a battle against history in Oklahoma, where voters haven’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in more than three decades. PRIMARY TAKEAWAYS: DEMS’ LEFT-CENTER BATTLE INTENSIFIES AS SCHUMER TAKES ANOTHER HIT; SPLIT DECISION FOR TRUMP And Thomas, who lists a host of policy proposals on her campaign website, including beefing up teacher pay, restoring Roe v. Wade, and expanding Obamacare, among other boilerplate Democratic proposals, also wants to accomplish one thing in the early days of her Senate career: impeaching Trump. During an interview with NPR affiliate KOSU last month, Thomas was asked about the Republican nominee, Rep. Kevin Hern, R-Okla., and his "fierce" backing of Trump, and how, if elected, she would approach a working relationship with the president. "Like I said, I'm kind, not nice. So I will make sure that I work as diligently as I can to make sure that within my first 100 days that we impeach, remove and convict," Thomas said. "They will have to pry that pen out of my cold, dead hands before I go any further with allowing this administration to continue doing what they're doing." DEM SENATE CANDIDATE CALLS TO 'SHUT THE WHITE HOUSE DOWN,' IMPEACH 2 SUPREME COURT JUSTICES "So, I mean, hopefully that's a good answer," she continued. "But I am going to remove, impeach, remove and convict. That's it. Like that's all. That's the answer." First, she’d have to survive Election Night in November against Hern, a tall task given that Trump won Oklahoma by nearly 35 points in 2024. Though Thomas has pulled off two underdog performances, earning roughly 45% of the vote during her first go-round for the Democratic nomination and then defeating Priest with no political experience, Hern is a different matter. DARLINE GRAHAM FACES MAKE-OR-BREAK GOP RUNOFF IN HISTORIC BID TO KEEP BROTHER’S SENATE SEAT He’s amassed an impressive campaign war chest that at one point peaked at nearly $10 million so far this cycle. Thomas, however, has raised just shy of $60,000. He also boasts the endorsement of Trump and has touted his desire to pass the president’s biggest policy priority, the SAVE America Act. Hern noted in a statement to Fox News Digital that Oklahomans "love President Trump and the America First Agenda." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Socialist Democrats like N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas are wildly out of touch with the values of Oklahomans and the direction they want our country moving toward," Hern said. "President Trump and Republicans are focused on delivering results. N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas and the radical left are focused on partisan politics against a president Oklahomans overwhelmingly elected."

articles.title: Trump endorsement boosts sister of late Lindsey Graham to historic runoff victory
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's endorsement and an $800,000 MAGA Inc. blitz helped Darline Graham defeat Ralph Norman in the South Carolina Senate runoff.
articles.body: A powerful name and an endorsement from President Donald Trump proved more than enough to score an unlikely candidate a win in the latest runoff election in South Carolina. Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., toppled Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., in a whirlwind race to replace her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, as the GOP nominee for the Senate after his sudden death in July. Just a little over a month after his death at 71 years old, South Carolinians opted to stick with a familiar name in Graham, who despite having little political experience prior to her appointment to finish out the remainder of her brother’s term, scored Trump’s coveted endorsement. DARLINE GRAHAM FACES MAKE-OR-BREAK GOP RUNOFF IN HISTORIC BID TO KEEP BROTHER’S SENATE SEAT Though her appointment by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster was viewed as temporary, Trump pushed her to run beyond the five months left in her brother’s term. "Darline is somebody I've known for a long time," Trump said during a rally for her in Myrtle Beach last week. "I asked her to do this. I said, ‘Darline, you got to do it,’ because everyone loves her. Everyone respects her." "So I've known her through Lindsey — I've known her for so long," he continued. "I think Lindsey respected Darline more than any other person he knows, including me." LINDSEY GRAHAM’S SISTER ADMITS SHE’S ‘NOT THAT INFORMED ON NATIONAL SECURITY’ WHILE SEEKING FULL SENATE TERM And Trump sent in last-minute financial reinforcements to help her, following a gaffe during her final debate with Norman when she admitted that she had little knowledge of the strategic importance of Taiwan. Graham has styled herself as a much different politician than her brother, focused more on domestic issues than foreign. Trump's mammoth, $400 million campaign war chest through MAGA Inc., which has largely been untapped this cycle despite a handful of Senate races shifting in power dynamics across the country, dumped over $800,000 into a phone campaign in support of Graham over the weekend, according to campaign finance records. While Graham styled herself as a more home front than abroad focused candidate, she made one thing clear through debates and limited campaign time: a vote for her was a vote for the Trump agenda. RALPH NORMAN SUGGESTS SPECIAL GOP PRIMARY RUNOFF RIVAL DARLINE GRAHAM IS THE ESTABLISHMENT'S CHOSEN CANDIDATE She targeted Norman for bucking House Republican leadership, and, at times, Trump, but noted, "We already have enough problem Democrats, we don’t need a problem Republican." And though she’s only been in the Senate for a handful of weeks, Graham argued to voters that she’d done more than Norman had in his entire congressional career, touting the passage of the long-awaited bipartisan Russia sanctions package initially pushed by her brother, but at times slowed by the White House. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I was in Washington for only two weeks before I passed the Russia and Iran Sanctions Act through the Senate," Graham said. "I then passed the deciding vote to confirm President Trump's attorney general, Todd Blanche." "Simply put, I've done more in 20 days than Ralph Norman has done in 20 years." Despite the bruising battle between Norman and Graham, Norman said he would be throwing his support behind her following his loss Tuesday, and planned to call Graham to say congratulations. "As I said earlier, I'm going to support the Republican. I'm not supporting a Democrat. So, I will support her – Darline – as best I can," Norman said during his concession speech Tuesday evening.

articles.title: Darline Graham wins GOP runoff to replace brother on South Carolina ballot: AP
articles.summary: Graham was endorsed by President Donald Trump.
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham -- a political newcomer appointed to the seat held by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham -- will win a special GOP primary runoff to replace her brother on the South Carolina ballot, the Associated Press projected Tuesday.

Graham, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated Rep. Ralph Norman, a staunch conservative and member of the hard line Freedom Caucus, who had also advanced to the runoff, following South Carolina's special Senate primary earlier this month.

Graham will face Democratic candidate Annie Andrews in November.

Speaking to a crowd of triumphant supporters Tuesday night in Columbia, South Carolina, Graham struck a reflective tone at times.

"The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it," she said, while adding that she was feeling "mixed emotions" given her grief over her brother.

As she thanked God, her key supporters and her family, Graham also effusively thanked Trump for his support and endorsement, describing the "bond" between her brother and the president and telling the crowd, to raucous cheers, "South Carolina is truly Trump country."

Graham framed her outsider status as an asset, while pointing to Trump's support as one of the key reasons conservatives should support her bid for a full term. Trump threw more than just a social media endorsement behind her: he flew to Myrtle Beach for a rally on Friday, in one of his first major campaign stops during the 2026 midterms.

"Now, the critics say I shouldn't run for the Senate. They say I'm not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged," Graham said during the rally to cheers. "And by the way, President Trump had never served in an elected office before, and I think he's done a damn good job."

Trump, later on, effusively praised Graham, saying "she only knows how to put America first."

South Carolina special Senate primary results: Lindsey Graham's sister Darline advances to Senate runoff

Norman, meanwhile, said that his experience is his "resume" and that conservatives in the Palmetto State could trust him more than a relative unknown like Graham.

"The establishment has already picked their candidate. Same old playbook, same old insiders. I'm not their choice. And this election is not for sale," he said in a campaign ad.

He also questioned why Trump has gotten involved in the race in GOP-favoring South Carolina instead of focusing on ones where the GOP faces an uphill battle against Democrats. The White House, asked about some of Norman's comments about Trump, pointed to Trump's previous social media posts where he endorsed Graham.

Graham, on her end, faced scrutiny from many fellow Republicans over her lack of political experience and occasional missteps on the trail.

Lindsey Graham, longtime senator from South Carolina and Trump ally, dies at 71

During a one-on-one debate she had with Norman last Tuesday, she was asked if Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the United States. She answered , "I'm not that informed on national security. But I do support the military ... I'm not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."

Darline Graham raises eyebrows after she says in debate she's 'not that informed on national security'

The comment, which contrasted with her brother's major focus on national security, sparked criticism from Norman's allies, including former Gov. Nikki Haley.

"Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States' national security. Darline Graham admits she's not. This is not something you inherit. And it's critical in the U.S. Senate," Haley wrote on X last week.

Norman, in an interview with local outlet WHNS posted on Thursday , called Graham's answer "surprising" and hammered her for her lack of experience:. "There's no more important issue than national security ... there's no time for training on the job," he said.

But Graham, while admitting she feels she got the answer wrong -- telling Fox News she "tripped up on one question" -- told voters at an event last week, "To me, as I've walked around this room and I've asked people, 'Are y'all concerned about Taiwan?' You know what they said? No, they're concerned about the price of groceries, the price of gas, rising healthcare costs."

She also said she believes national security is important and she will become more informed about it. "Everybody has a first day on the job. President Trump -- was he a politician [when he was first elected]? Has he done a good job? Yes, he has," she told attendees.

Heading into the runoff, David Woodard, a political scientist who also managed some of Lindsey Graham's early congressional campaigns, but did not work on this Senate race, told ABC News that he expected relatively low turnout and that those showing up to vote in such an off-cycle election are likely among the most opinionated, plugged-in Republicans.

"I think on the first round, people I was talking to had sympathy for Darline, thought it was great she'd serve out Lindsey's term," he said, adding that some of them "think that Ralph Norman has credibility on issues that Darline lacks."

But heading into Tuesday some voters said they find Trump's endorsement of her, as well as her focus on the economy, a strong selling point.

Mike Funderburk, a contractor from Neeses, South Carolina, who voted early for Graham, said the economy is his top issue.

"I think she's probably going to have a steep learning curve," he said. "But I'm willing to give her the benefit of the doubt."

ABC News' Michelle Stoddart contributed to this report.

articles.title: Capitol Police seize guillotine from pickup truck
articles.summary: U.S. Capitol Police on Tuesday arrested a man after discovering a guillotine in the bed of a pickup truck parked on the eastern edge of the National Mall. Officers first spotted an illegally parked pickup truck along the 100 block of East Capitol St. —near the Capitol building, the Supreme Court and the Library of…
articles.body:
U.S. Capitol Police on Tuesday arrested a man after discovering a guillotine in the bed of a pickup truck parked on the eastern edge of the National Mall.

Officers first spotted an illegally parked pickup truck along the 100 block of East Capitol St. —near the Capitol building, the Supreme Court and the Library of Congress, the department said in a statement . It was there they also found a multi-foot tall guillotine, shown in pictures shared by Capitol Police.

The guillotine was seized and officers arrested Philan-Tam-Duy Le, 35, of Julian, Calif. — a town located about 60 miles northeast of San Diego. Le faces one count of carrying a dangerous weapon.

Capitol Police investigators “are going through the suspect’s background to learn more about why he came to Washington, D.C.”

Guillotines were fashioned as the primary method of execution during the French Revolution in the late 1790s. During the “Reign of Terror,” the weapon was used to kill thousands — including French nobles, King Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette.

France continued to use the device into the 20th century, as late as 1977, before the country outlawed capital punishment four years later.

articles.title: Hochul remains defiant after sheriffs sue over law banning cooperation with ICE: 'Bring it on'
articles.summary: More than a dozen New York sheriffs are suing state officials over a new state law that prohibits law enforcement from cooperating with ICE.
articles.body: More than a dozen New York sheriffs are suing over a state law prohibiting law enforcement from entering into or maintaining certain agreements with ICE for civil immigration enforcement, as Gov. Kathy Hochul dared the agency heads to "bring it on." A federal lawsuit led by Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault argues that the law is unconstitutional and unlawfully restricts elected sheriffs’ ability to enter into federally authorized immigration-enforcement agreements. "Today, Kathy Hochul escalated her administration’s war on the police and she expanded polices to put criminals before the citizens of New York," Rensselaer County Executive Steve McLaughlin said on Tuesday. The Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, which Hochul signed in May, took effect on Tuesday, barring local and state law enforcement agencies from entering into partnerships with federal authorities to assist on civil immigration matters. The law also bars new agreements to house civil immigration detainees; existing detention agreements must be terminated under their applicable termination provisions within three months of the law’s effective date. BORDER CZAR HOMAN VOWS TO 'FLOOD' NEW YORK WITH ICE AGENTS DESPITE HOCHUL'S RESISTANCE Police may still assist ICE in cases of violent or other forms of non-immigration crime, but officers may not divert local resources to help with civil immigration enforcement as part of an effort to advance President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. Hochul threatened to sue localities that refuse to end cooperation agreements with ICE, setting up a confrontation between herself and her Republican challenger, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, as his county is among those with agreements with ICE. "No county executive should think that they are above the law in the state of New York," Hochul said at a press conference on Tuesday. She said any police department or sheriff’s office that ignores the law and maintains an agreement with ICE will face legal action. "And to those suing us, those trying to block the implementation of this law who’ve tried before and failed, our law has already been upheld by the courts, but if you try me again, I say, bring it on," the governor declared. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS New York Attorney General Letitia James also issued subpoenas to law enforcement agencies that either did not confirm plans to end their agreements or failed to provide what her office viewed as a satisfactory response. The subpoenas were sent to the sheriff's offices of Broome, Steuben, Nassau and Rensselaer counties, as well as the Nassau County Police Department. If the agencies fail to comply, the attorney general is vowing to file a civil suit, a spokesperson for her office told CBS News. Hochul has said law enforcement will assist ICE "only if a real crime has been committed" but officers cannot use resources to help on civil immigration matters. "Because we need local cops hunting down criminals, not kindergartners. Breaking up drug rings, not breaking up families. Arresting gun runners, not grandmas," Hochul said. Blakeman, who held a press conference at the same time as Hochul's, did not address whether he would comply with the state's orders, but he later told the New York Post he would "probably" join the sheriffs' lawsuit. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He has previously defended working with ICE to remove illegal immigrants, claiming at a recent event with Trump that about 2,000 of these individuals in his county have criminal records. "Kathy Hochul, where do you want those guns? What neighborhood do you want to destroy? Where do you want those drugs? What community do you want to destroy? Where do you want those illegal immigrants with criminal records to live? You want it back in New York? We say no," Blakeman said at the time. The Department of Homeland Security said Hochul "must stop putting politics above public safety." "This type of insanity leads to more crimes and more innocent victims," a department spokesperson told the New York Post.

articles.title: Man arrested after guillotine is found in pickup truck near Capitol
articles.summary: Capitol Police said investigators were looking into why the 35-year-old suspect from California was in Washington.
articles.body: U.S. Capitol Police on Tuesday arrested a man who they say was carrying a guillotine in the bed of a pickup truck. Philan-Tam-Duy Le of Julian, California, was arrested on suspicion of “carrying a dangerous weapon” and being in possession of the guillotine, Capitol Police said in a news release. Police said Le, 35, drove to Washington from California. “USCP investigators are going through the suspect’s background to learn more about why he came to Washington,” police said in their news release. Le’s truck was spotted near the Capitol and the Supreme Court, where officers say it was illegally parked. Congress is in recess, meaning lawmakers are in their home districts, not in Washington. An Instagram account that appeared to belong to Le included a Story on Tuesday afternoon featuring a video of a man with the guillotine outside FBI headquarters in Washington. “Outside the FBI building, just eating some cheese pizza,” the man says in the video. The post included the caption “Guillotine adventures” and said, “Capital hill next.” Capitol Police often make arrests beyond the Capitol grounds, and those incidents are not necessarily politically motivated.

articles.title: Dolly Parton refused to pick political sides for decades: ‘I’m not in politics, I’m an entertainer’
articles.summary: Dolly Parton, who died Tuesday at 80, built a career on refusing to take political sides despite repeated pressure involving Trump and Clinton.
articles.body: Dolly Parton spent decades singing about love, heartbreak, faith and working "9 to 5," but there was one arena the country music legend repeatedly resisted entering: partisan politics. "I am not political, and I refuse to get caught up in political things," Parton told USA Today in a 2020 interview. Parton, who died Tuesday at 80, maintained that position through the presidential elections, pointed questions about President Donald Trump, offers of the nation's highest civilian honor and controversies involving some of her fellow entertainers. KENNY CHESNEY TELLS BILL MAHER THE KEY REASON HE REFUSES TO TELL HIS LISTENERS HOW TO VOTE "I don't like to get involved in politics, because first of all, I have as many Republican fans as I do Democrats," Parton told USA Today. "I don't want to offend anybody, I have a right to myself." "Like God gave us free will, America gave us free speech, but you've got to be responsible for anything you say and do," she added. Two years earlier, Parton was repeatedly pressed about Trump during an interview with ABC's David Wright, according to the Knoxville News Sentinel. DWAYNE 'THE ROCK' JOHNSON REJECTS HOLLYWOOD’S POLITICAL OBSESSION, BLASTS CELEBRITY ATTACK CULTURE "I have a lot of fans out there, and I don’t want to offend anybody," Parton said. When Wright attempted to draw a parallel between Trump and the sexually abusive boss in Parton's 1980 film "9 to 5," she refused to bite. "I’m not addressing that," Parton said. "I learned a long time ago, keep your damn mouth shut if you want to stay in show business. … I’m not in politics, I’m an entertainer." When Wright pointed out that Parton was also a role model, she responded: "Yes I am. That’s why I don’t talk about people." JOHNNY CARSON'S FRIEND SAYS LATE-NIGHT KING WISELY AVOIDED PARTISANSHIP AS KIMMEL CONTROVERSY GROWS Parton's determination to avoid partisan politics with one of America's highest honors. She revealed in 2021 that the Trump administration had twice offered her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Parton said she declined the first offer because her husband, Carl Dean, was ill and the second because she would not travel during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the BBC. By then, the Biden administration had also approached her about the award. "Now I feel like if I take it, it'll be doing politics, so I'm not so sure," Parton told NBC's "Today." MICK JAGGER DOESN'T WANT TO 'LECTURE' FANS, SAYS HIS JOB IS TO MAKE PEOPLE 'HAVE THE BEST TIME'  Her aversion to political camps did not mean she kept quiet about everything she believed. "I know whatever I say, people are going to listen, and they’re going to make more of it than maybe what I meant. So I have to be careful," Parton told People in 2021. "Of course I have my opinion, but I’m not an opinionated person as a rule. You’re allowed your own beliefs and your own faith, but you don’t have to use it like a weapon when it could be a tool." Parton's political neutrality was something she could joke about. "My daddy was a Republican, my mama was a Democrat, and I’m a hypocrite!" Parton famously quipped, pronouncing 'hypocrite' as 'hypo-crat' in her iconic Tennessee drawl. DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80 Parton's philosophy was tested again when she recorded a duet with Kid Rock for her 2023 album, "Rockstar." Parton defended working with the conservative musician after she was questioned about the collaboration, telling The Hollywood Reporter that she had recorded the song before a controversy involving Kid Rock but would likely have worked with him anyway, according to Rolling Stone. "Hey, just because I love you don’t mean I don’t love Kid Rock. Just because I love Kid Rock don’t mean I don’t love you," Parton said. "I don’t condemn or criticize. I just accept and love." Parton said she still would "probably" have recorded the duet because she considered Kid Rock talented and believed accepting someone did not require agreeing with everything they did. BILLY RAY CYRUS URGES PRAYER FOR TRUMP, SAYS BEING COMMANDER IN CHIEF IS A 'TOUGH JOB' "I think that’s terrible," Parton said, according to Rolling Stone. "We all make mistakes. We don’t all get caught at it." Parton tied that belief to her Christian faith, arguing that people deserved forgiveness and second chances. "I ask God every day to let Him shine through me. He’s given me that gift to be able to talk to them, and I’m very careful with it. And people don’t really come to see me be me — they come to see me be them, the parts of me they can relate to," she told People in 2021. During the 2016 presidential campaign, Parton clarified that she had not endorsed Hillary Clinton after comments she made about the Democratic nominee were interpreted as an endorsement, according to the Knoxville News Sentinel. Asked later about the race between Clinton and Trump, Parton jokingly called the campaign "the greatest show on television," and described both candidates as "nuts." Even running for president herself wasn't entertained by the iconic entertainer for a moment. "No. I don’t think anybody could actually do a great job at that," Parton told Metro in 2023, according to People. "I think we’ve had enough ‘boobs’ in the White House." Parton said she preferred trying to make a difference through music and the way she treated others. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I’m not smart enough to be in politics, or maybe I’m too smart," she said. "Either way, I’m not qualified for that type of a job. But I’m pretty qualified to do what I do, which is to point people in the right direction, to write about it in songs or speak about things." Parton died after a "brief battle with cancer," according to her representatives. At her request, a small, private service will be held for her immediate family, with the family asking for donations to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library rather than flowers.

articles.title: Trump-backed Mazzei defeats Drummond in Oklahoma governor GOP runoff
articles.summary: Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei (R) is projected to defeat state Attorney General Gentner Drummond (R) in the Republican primary runoff for Oklahoma governor — a win for President Trump who backed Mazzei in the contest, according to Decision Desk HQ. Drummond and Mazzei, a financial planner, were vying for the GOP nod to…
articles.body:
Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei (R) is projected to defeat state Attorney General Gentner Drummond (R) in the Republican primary runoff for Oklahoma governor — a win for President Trump who backed Mazzei in the contest, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Drummond and Mazzei, a financial planner, were vying for the GOP nod to succeed term-limited Gov. Kevin Stitt (R). It’s a critical victory for Trump after several of his initial primary picks in Iowa, Georgia, Minnesota, South Carolina and Wyoming lost their elections earlier this year, raising questions about the power of the president’s endorsement.

Stitt and his wife also donated to Mazzei.

Meanwhile, the Oklahoma attorney general received endorsements from the Oklahoma State Fraternal Order of Police, House Speaker Pro Tempore Anthony Moore (R) and former University of Oklahoma football coach Barry Switzer.

Mazzei narrowly trailed Drummond in the initial GOP primary, and some recent polling showed a tight race.

Both candidates also saw millions of dollars poured into their campaigns: Between contributions, loans and money from political action committees, the Oklahoma attorney general raised $10 million overall, according to a pre-primary runoff state campaign finance report.

Meanwhile, Mazzei amassed close to $12.5 million, including a $11 million self-loan, according to his pre-primary runoff state campaign report.

Ahead of the Tuesday primary, Trump attacked Drummond as a “fake Republican,” hitting him for opposing a planned aluminum smelter, which was backed by the president. He also ripped the GOP nominee for campaign contributions to former President Biden, among others.

Drummond has said that an erroneous $1,000 contribution given to the Biden campaign in 2020 was mistakenly made by his wife through their joint account and later refunded, according to Oklahoma Watch .

articles.title: Trump nabs crucial primary wins in South Carolina, Oklahoma: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: President Trump notched two critical wins in South Carolina and Oklahoma on Tuesday, with Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.) and former state Sen. Mike Mazzei (Okla.) clinching the GOP nominations in their respective primary runoff races. The Republican contests for South Carolina Senate and Oklahoma governor served as another key test of the president’s influence in the GOP as several of his gubernatorial and House picks have…
articles.body:
President Trump notched two critical wins in South Carolina and Oklahoma on Tuesday, with Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.) and former state Sen. Mike Mazzei (Okla.) clinching the GOP nominations in their respective primary runoff races.

The Republican contests for South Carolina Senate and Oklahoma governor served as another key test of the president’s influence in the GOP as several of his gubernatorial and House picks have fallen short in their primaries this cycle.

Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) by nearly 5 percentage points while Mazzei eked out Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond by about half a point, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Graham, who was appointed to serve the remainder of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.), term in the upper chamber, faced growing questions around her lack of political experience after a gaffe on the debate stage last week.

But Trump’s endorsement carried both her and Mazzei across the finish line, underscoring the president’s firm grip on the party in key contests ahead of the November midterms. Trump had ripped Mazzei’s opponent in the days ahead of Tuesday’s contest.

Meanwhile, a democratic socialist won the Democratic nod for Senate in Oklahoma, while a new Georgia Democrat is heading to Washington, D.C. , to fill the remainder of the late Rep. David Scott’s (D) term.

Here are the key takeaways from Tuesday’s elections:

Trump’s successful coronation in South Carolina

Graham pulled it off in South Carolina — helping Trump avoid an embarrassing primary loss.

Trump threw his political weight behind the incumbent and visited the state last week to rally alongside Graham. His super PAC MAGA Inc. also invested $827,000 in the contest, marking the group’s largest investment so far this election cycle.

“South Carolina is truly Trump country,” Darline Graham told supporters during her victory speech on Tuesday.

“Lindsey truly loved you and viewed you as one of his closest friends. I appreciate that bond and appreciate all that you’ve done for our country,” she said, directing her remarks to Trump. “Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful.”

Polling released ahead of Tuesday’s contest showed the incumbent and Norman effectively tied after a stumble on the debate stage last week sparked speculation that Graham could potentially fall short on Tuesday.

In response to a question from the debate moderator about Taiwan and the South China Sea, Graham replied, “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security.”

“But I do support the military,” she added.

Norman seized the moment, contrasting his near decade in the House with the incumbent’s political inexperience. But several Republicans, including South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) and the president, came to her defense.

“She’s very smart, and she was being honest. She’s into the price of groceries … She is going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump told reporters Friday.

Graham’s win is particularly notable given the president’s initial gubernatorial pick — South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette (R) — lost. He had also backed Attorney General Alan Wilson in the race, but the outcome prompted questions about whether South Carolina Republicans would buck the president’s endorsee again.

The Republican nominee will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in the general election.

Trump bucks gubernatorial losing streak in Oklahoma

Trump came out on top in a tight Oklahoma governor’s GOP runoff with Mazzei’s victory over Drummond.

The president’s endorsement track record has been spotty in gubernatorial primaries this year. His initial picks for governor in Minnesota , Iowa , South Carolina , Georgia and Wyoming were all defeated.

He also notched a handful of high-profile primary losses in the House this month, including GOP Reps. Andy Ogles (Tenn.) and Cory Mills (Fla.) None of his choices for the Senate have lost their primaries so far this year.

Still, he president boasted his primary scorecard earlier this week, writing that his “endorsements are stronger than ever” on social media.

Drummond narrowly led Mazzei in the initial June primary runoff. The race took a nasty turn, with Mazzei releasing a drug test this week after public pressure from Drummond, who did the same.

In the days ahead of the runoff, Trump also hammered the attorney general , calling him a “fake Republican.” Drummond, a rancher, opposed a Trump-backed aluminum plant in the state and in recent days has slammed the president’s decision to import beef and tariff Canadian goods.

“I’m unafraid to disagree with the president when he’s wrong, and he’s wrong on tariffs, He’s wrong on importing cheap beef,” Drummond told NewsNation Sunday.

Mazzei will face Democrat Cyndi Munson, the minority leader of the state House, in November.

Socialist wins primary in the Sooner State

Democratic socialists notched another win Tuesday — this time in Oklahoma.

N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas is projected to secure the Democratic nomination to take on Rep. Kevin Hern (R) for Senate. She defeated Jim Priest, a centrist Democrat, to clinch the nod in the ruby red state.

Although Thomas, a nurse, is unlikely to win in November — an Oklahoma Democrat has not served in the Senate since 1994 — her victory underscores the surging energy on the left this primary cycle.

Progressives and democratic socialists have knocked out incumbents and clinched key party nominations across the country this year. In Florida, state Rep. Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist, pulled off on upset to take on Republican Sen. Ashley Moody this fall, while progressive Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens for the Democratic nod for Michigan Senate. El-Sayed does not identify as a socialist.

Concerns from the Democratic establishment, however, have dominated conversation , with some party leaders arguing more moderate candidates are better equipped to take on Republicans in general elections in battleground and red states.

But recent polling suggests that Democrats view socialism more favorably than capitalism and that a third of Democrats identify as democratic socialists.

New Georgia Democrat heads to Capitol Hill

The late Rep. David Scott’s daughter was defeated in the special election runoff for his Atlanta-based seat.

David Scott was first elected to Congress in 2002 and later served as the first Black chair of the House Agriculture Committee. He passed away in April at age 80.

Former Gwinnett County Board of Education chair Everton Blair is poised to defeat Marcye Scott by about 6 percentage points, with 95 percent of the vote reported as of late Tuesday.

Marcye Scott led Blair by just over 10 points in the initial special election in July. Marcye Scott was backed by Democratic Reps. Maxine Waters (Calif.) and Nikema Williams (Ga.), while Blair notched support from Georgia Rep. Lucy McBath (D).

Blair will only serve on Capitol Hill for a handful of months. Democratic state Rep. Jasmine Clark won the May primary for the full two-year term for David Scott’s seat, and she is expected to easily win in the blue stronghold this November.

Blair will join Democrat Aisha Wahab as new members of the 119th Congress when the House is back in session Wahab narrowly won a special election last week for former Rep. Eric Swalwell’s seat in California. The former congressman resigned amid sexual assault allegations, which he has denied. Wahab is running for a full two-year term in November.

It is unclear what date Blair and Wahab will be sworn in by Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.). The House returns from recess on Aug. 31.

Once the pair of Democrats are inducted, the minority will increase from 212 to 214 members. Republicans currently hold the majority with 218 seats.

Julia Mueller contributed to this report. Updated at 10:58 p.m. EDT

articles.title: Trump-backed Mike Mazzei wins the GOP nomination in the Oklahoma governor’s race
articles.summary: Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei has secured the Republican nomination for governor in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump’s preferred candidate.
articles.body: Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei has secured the Republican nomination for governor in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump’s preferred candidate. Mazzei narrowly defeated state Attorney General Gentner Drummond by about 2,000 votes in the GOP primary runoff. The initial June primary was also tight. Drummond finished in first place by just more than 1,000 votes over Mazzei. Since no candidate in the crowded field secured a majority, the race went to a runoff. In the weeks leading up to the runoff, Drummond outraised and outspent Mazzei, with his campaign reporting last week that he brought in $2.3 million between the mid-June primary and Tuesday’s runoff. Mazzei, in the same time period, raised $816,000. Both candidates have also loaned their campaigns significant sums: $11 million for Mazzei and $3 million for Drummond. Trump first endorsed Mazzei in May in the race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Kevin Stitt and continued to reiterate his support for the former state lawmaker. In a post on Truth Social last week, Trump praised Mazzei and criticized Drummond, writing, “Drummond is not the right guy. He’s got a bad attitude, and he doesn’t stand for the Values of Oklahoma, which must VOTE FOR ‘MIKE MAZZEI FOR GOVERNOR,’ on Tuesday, August 25th.” Drummond also drew the president’s ire for suing to block the construction of the largest aluminum smelter in the country in Inola, Oklahoma, citing environmental and public health concerns. “He wants to dethrone a magnificent, Job producing, desperately needed, and brand new, Aluminum Plant that will be one of the best projects ever conceived or built, not only in the Great State of Oklahoma, but in the United States, itself,” Trump wrote in the Truth Social post earlier this month. Mazzei, on the other hand, supports construction of the plant. This week, Drummond also broke with the president on his decision last week to waive tariffs on some beef imports in an attempt to lower beef prices in the U.S. “I think Oklahoma and I are supportive of President Trump and many of his policies. I do think the majority of Oklahomans would agree that the tariffs are too far, that importing cheap beef only injures Oklahoma’s cattlemen, ranchers and farmers,” Drummond told NewsNation, echoing the concerns of GOP lawmakers in the House and Senate from states with large cattle-ranching communities. While Trump’s endorsement remains the most coveted in GOP politics, he has had some stumbles, particularly in governor’s races. Five gubernatorial candidates he has backed this year failed to win their primaries. With his victory Tuesday, Mazzei is the heavy favorite to win November’s general election, given the state’s deeply Republican voter base. He’ll face Democratic state Rep. Cyndi Munson in the general election.

articles.title: Judge strikes down Texas ban on drag shows, tells people offended by them ‘just don’t go’
articles.summary: The federal judge, who cited Dolly Parton in his ruling, found that the state law violated the First Amendment.
articles.body: A federal judge in Texas struck down a 2023 state law Tuesday that sought to restrict drag shows, ruling it was unconstitutional. U.S. District Judge David Hittner, a Reagan appointee, said the measure, known as Texas Senate Bill 12, improperly restricted speech, violating the First Amendment of the Constitution. The ruling prevents state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for the Senate, from enforcing the law and denies his motion for a new trial. In the ruling, Hittner also had advice for “those who find such activities as described in this case offensive.” “The solution is relatively simple ... just don’t go,” he wrote. Paxton’s office did not immediately reply to a request for comment Tuesday night. The state law would fine business owners who were found to be in violation up to $10,000 for hosting events, while performers could be charged with a Class A misdemeanor, which could result in up to one year of jail time. The statute, which has been the source of a yearslong legal battle, has made its way to Hittner’s courtroom before. Hittner first deemed it unconstitutional and a violation of the First Amendment in 2023, but the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals returned it to him in November, lifting a pause on the law and giving him specific instructions about how to reassess it. It went back into effect last year following the appeals court ruling. Texas is among a handful of states that have passed legislation to restrict drag shows. Hittner struck down the law Tuesday after having followed the framework the higher court asked him to follow. In his ruling, Hittner mentioned Dolly Parton, whose death was announced Tuesday, and criticized the law’s definition of banning performances that “[appeal] to the prurient interest,” citing people who would chastise Parton “as a voluptuous sex symbol because of her big hair, flamboyant clothes and breast exposure.” “There are ‘erotic’ elements in countless popular performances that could be subject to both civil and criminal penalties under S.B. 12,” he wrote. One of the plaintiffs in the case, a drag queen who performs under the name Brigitte Bandit, impersonates Parton in her performances. Bandit celebrated the ruling on social media Tuesday, posting a screenshot of the decision and captioning it, “Drag is free speech, b----.” She announced she would also perform as Parton, who gave her a rhinestone guitar as a gift in 2023, at an Austin bar Saturday in her honor. Hittner added that the law was so overly broad as to lead even activities such as “cheerleading, dancing, live theater, and other common public occurrences” to be treated as civil or criminal violations. He also said that the law was vague on its face and that it failed “to give a reasonable person notice of what is prohibited.”

articles.title: Trump-endorsed candidate clears key hurdle in red state gubernatorial race
articles.summary: Mike Mazzei secured Trump's endorsement and defeated Genter Drummond in Oklahoma's GOP governor runoff, promising to eliminate the state's income tax.
articles.body: Mike Mazzei, a former Oklahoma state senator and financial planner, won a primary election runoff on Tuesday evening with the backing of President Donald Trump to secure the GOP nomination for governor in Oklahoma. Having beaten out Genter Drummond, the current Oklahoma attorney general, Mazzei is now the heavy favorite to become the Sooner State’s next governor. His win is also a political victory for outgoing Gov. Kevin Stitt, who has opposed Drummond for years. Stitt and Drummond have sparred over lawsuits, pointed letters and public criticisms. At one point, Stitt even described Drummond as a "longtime political enemy" in a quote to local outlets. TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SPARKS RUNOFF AGAINST POPULAR PROSECUTOR IN KEY GUBERNATORIAL RACE The feud between them centers on Drummond’s attacks of Oklahoma poultry companies for what he sees as decades of phosphorus pollution in water supplies. Stitt has rebuffed those characterizations, calling them an overreach of Drummond’s role as attorney general and warning that litigation against the companies could threaten jobs and the agricultural industry of the state. Stitt endorsed Mazzei, stating that "we want a pro-business governor in there to take the lead for the next four years." Stitt is prevented by term limits from running again. His exit prompted a crowded field of hopefuls to replace him, but after an initial primary on June 2, no candidate secured the 50% support needed to lock up the nomination outright. Only Drummond and Mazzei advanced to a runoff. Like Stitt, President Donald Trump also endorsed Mazzei, calling him a "MAGA warrior." "As a successful Businessman, and former Chairman of the State Senate Finance Committee, and later, as Oklahoma’s Secretary of Budget, Mike knows the AMERICA FIRST Policies required to Grow our Economy, Create GREAT Jobs, Cut Taxes and Regulations, Promote MADE IN THE U.S.A., and Unleash American Energy DOMINANCE," Trump wrote in a May post to Truth Social. TRUMP-BACKED FIREBRAND WINS ARIZONA GOP GOVERNOR PRIMARY, SETTING UP HIGH-STAKES SHOWDOWN Mazzei based his campaign on promises to cut taxes, among other state-government reforms. "I have a detailed plan to eliminate Oklahoma’s income tax in six years. I have a plan to eliminate property taxes for seniors and veterans," Mazzei said in a campaign video posted to Instagram. In addition to tax reforms, Mazzei highlighted preventing foreign nationals from buying up state land, bolstering the Oklahoma education system and government spending accountability. In turn, Mazzei tried to paint Drummond as a fake Republican with a penchant for expanding government. "His solution to every problem is to raise taxes and grow government," Mazzei said. "He doesn’t understand money and finance. Crunching numbers is a skill you pick up when you earn your wealth rather than inherit it." In his own campaign, Drummond, a multigenerational rancher and former fighter pilot, highlighted his record as attorney general. On his website, he touted having confronted Chinese criminal operations growing illegal marijuana farms, shutting down thousands of their illegal grow operations and enforcing immigration law. "As a tough-on-crime attorney general and decorated fighter pilot, I have proven I will always fight for our freedom and defend our values," Drummond said in a campaign video. TRUMP SWITCHES SUPPORT IN OKLAHOMA CONGRESSIONAL RACE AS FORMERLY ENDORSED PASTOR CANDIDATE SUSPENDS CAMPAIGN "I’ll keep standing strong with President Trump to secure the border, deport illegals and stop the flow of drugs and crime," Drummond said. The Club for Growth, a pro-small-government group that advocates for lower taxes and free-market principles and contributed $9 million in support of Mazzei, praised his win. "Mike Mazzei is a principled conservative who will advocate for lower taxes, fewer regulations, and for Oklahoma parents to have a voice in their children’s education," Club for Growth PAC President David McIntosh said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Meanwhile, Gentner Drummond has spent his career putting radical education bureaucrats ahead of families by opposing school freedom. The message is clear, if you oppose school freedom and call yourself a Republican, expect to lose your next primary." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Having cleared the primary, Mazzei will face off against Democratic nominee Cyndi Munson, House minority leader in the Oklahoma House of Representatives. The general election is set for Nov. 3.

articles.title: The second Dan Sullivan makes the general election in Alaska’s Senate race
articles.summary: NBC News projects that GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Republican Dan J. Sullivan will face off in the general election alongside former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat.
articles.body: Former teacher Dan J. Sullivan will join Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola on the general election ballot in Alaska’s Senate race, NBC News projects. Republicans have criticized the other Sullivan’s candidacy as a potential ploy to confuse voters in a key battleground race, which he has denied. Alaska’s election system might also blunt the impact of any confusion. The top four candidates, regardless of party, advance from Alaska’s all-party primary to a ranked-choice general election, meaning voters could rank both Sullivans. But some voters end up ranking only one candidate, which could matter in a close race — and Alaska’s Senate race could be one of the closest in the country this year. Democrats have targeted Alaska as an opportunity to flip a seat since well before the same-name saga consumed the race, even though President Donald Trump carried the state by double digits in each of the last three presidential elections. Peltola, a former state legislator and city council member, became the first Alaska Native to represent the state in Congress when she won a statewide special election in 2022 and then a full term months later. Peltola lost her seat after one term by 3 percentage points, running well ahead of Vice President Kamala Harris at the top of the Democratic ticket in 2024. Sullivan was first elected to the Senate in 2014, defeating a Democratic incumbent, and re-elected in 2020. A former Marine, he has touted his work for veterans and the state’s fishing industry. His campaign and Republican allies have criticized the other Sullivan as a potential Democratic plant, noting that he only recently registered as a Republican and got help with his campaign launch from a Democratic consultant. State and federal prosecutors are investigating whether his candidacy is part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. The federal investigation is moving forward, with a law enforcement official telling NBC News that a grand jury issued subpoenas last week to compel information from witnesses related to the Dan J. Sullivan campaign. The candidate told The New York Times that he registered as a Republican because his previous political party, the Alaska Independence Party, no longer exists. He declined to detail his involvement with the Democratic consultant because of the ongoing investigation.

articles.title: Trump admin pauses visa appointments worldwide amid heightened screening for applicants
articles.summary: The State Department paused all visa interviews at embassies and consulates worldwide as officers undergo training on new public charge guidance.
articles.body: The Trump administration has directed U.S. embassies and consulates around the world to postpone immigrant visa interviews while consular officers complete training on new public-charge guidance, temporarily stalling applications that have reached the interview stage. The State Department told diplomatic posts to reschedule immigrant visa interviews until consular officers complete the training on how to evaluate whether an applicant is likely to become a public charge. A public-charge determination can make an immigrant visa applicant inadmissible under federal immigration law if officials determine the person is likely to become dependent on certain forms of public assistance after arriving in the U.S. "In early August, we launched a global training initiative at all of our embassies and consulates worldwide. To accommodate this in-depth training, appointments for visa services will be adjusted," a State Department official said in a statement. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES SIX-FIGURE PRICE TAG FOR NEW H-1B VISAS The official added that the training is intended to ensure evaluations of visa applicants are made "comprehensively and consistently." For most diplomatic posts, the training sessions are expected to take place this week. The State Department did not say when affected applicants would be notified of their rescheduled interview dates. The scheduling changes have sparked uncertainty among immigrant visa applicants who received emails informing them that their interviews had been canceled without instructions for immediately rescheduling them. STATE DEPARTMENT BLASTS BACK AT 'ROGUE JUDGE' WHO OVERTURNED AGGRESSIVE VISA CRACKDOWN Applicants were told they would receive future notice of a new interview date but were not given a timeline for when that communication could be expected. The move comes as President Donald Trump pursues a broader immigration crackdown that has extended beyond illegal immigration to legal immigration pathways. While Trump campaigned in 2024 on curbing illegal immigration, his administration has also imposed additional restrictions on legal immigration, including higher fees for certain work visas and new limits on how long some foreign students and journalists can remain in the US. The administration has also pursued visa revocations and removal proceedings in cases involving political activity and speech, including some anti-Israel activists. Those efforts have prompted court challenges alleging violations of free-speech and due-process protections. The administration said Monday that it was preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the U.S., a move that would represent the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history. On Friday, a federal judge struck down a State Department policy suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, ruling that the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio's statutory authority. articles.title: Armenia announces historic intention to apply for EU membership
articles.summary: Armenia’s Pashinyan laid out Yerevan's decision to formally apply for EU membership “in the near future” and to call for a national referendum, challenging R...
articles.body:
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told the country's lawmakers on Monday that Armenia would begin preparing to apply for EU membership, in a historic geopolitical shift for a country formerly in Russia's orbit and for the South Caucasus as a whole.

In a speech to parliament and the nation, Pashinyan said Armenia would decide its future through a referendum only after formally applying to join the EU, with a timeframe he described as "in the near future".

In a calculated set of political moves, the Armenian premier said his government would wait for Brussels' answer to its application, then discuss the roadmap for EU accession negotiations, and only then put EU membership to a national referendum.

Currently a member of the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO), Armenia was given an ultimatum a few months ago from alliance members to choose between continuing its membership or taking its own path toward the EU through a national referendum.

At the time, Pashinyan said it was premature to make such a decision, in the midst of a massive Russian onslaught of economic restrictions on the former Soviet state for daring to move out of its influence, with Russian president Vladimir Putin threatening Yerevan directly with a "Ukrainian scenario," as EU and CSTO membership would be incompatible in the Kremlin's view.

But in his groundbreaking speech on Monday, Pashinyan said, "I would be very glad if the organisation decided to remove the Republic of Armenia from the Collective Security Treaty Organisation," adding that "at least that would free us from the dilemma of whether or not to leave."

However, Pashinyan made it clear that Armenia would remain in the CSTO for the time being, until the choice between the Russia-led alliance and the EU "becomes unavoidable".

"For two centuries, Armenian-Russian relations have been built on the foundation and understanding that Russia is the guarantor of the security of the Armenian people and the Armenian state," Pashinyan said, describing the current trajectory of his view on Russia's role in Armenia's future.

"The developments of 2021, 2022 and 2023 showed that, due to its own security challenges, the Russian Federation can at times face significant limitations in its ability to perform this role," he added in reference to Armenia's wars with Azerbaijan over Karabakh, which since then ended with a historic peace process between the two former rivals.

"This is where we once again came face to face with the fact that we have failed to learn the lessons of our history," the Armenian prime minister said of his vision of Russia's role in Armenia's future — a statement which he has repeated several times, pointing at the Kremlin for giving up on Armenia during its last confrontation with Azerbaijan.

After signing the peace process in August 2025, Armenia and Azerbaijan embarked on a future of economic cooperation and stability that the two former foes are forging ahead together on their own, with significant EU and US participation.

Armenia's economy still relies on Russian energy and infrastructure, but in another surprise move on Monday, Pashinyan asked Moscow to give up its monopoly concession of Armenian railways which runs until 2038 so that Yerevan can integrate its rail into international networks, with either Kazakhstan or the UAE as possible investors.

Russia responded swiftly to Pashinyan's historic statements, with the Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov announcing that Armenia's alignment with EU standards may trigger what he called "deep trade contradictions that will primarily harm Armenia."

As for its departure from the CSTO, "if Yerevan no longer needs membership in such an important organisation for ensuring regional security due to its national interests, it is free to make the corresponding decision and leave this organisation," Peskov said, signalling that the Kremlin was setting the stage for a turbulent path ahead with its former ally.

articles.title: Michigan GOP lawmaker casts doubt on El-Sayed’s socialist denial as policies tell another story: ‘Sharp odds’
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed denies the socialist label, but a Michigan lawmaker says his policies on ICE, Medicare for All, and taxing billionaires say otherwise.
articles.body: Despite Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed denying ties to socialism, a Republican Michigan lawmaker warned his policy agenda tells a different story and predicted voters will reject it in November. "Abdul El-Sayed can't define what a woman is, so I'm not surprised he can't define what socialist is," Michigan state Rep. Bill G. Schuette told Fox News Digital. "The facts are all the policies he supports are emblematic of the DSA movement and of this really far-left socialist idea." El-Sayed, a former public health official, narrowly defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., securing an upset victory for the party’s progressive wing in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary earlier this month. His nomination follows multiple primary victories by candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), including in New York, Florida and Colorado. DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE While El-Sayed has pushed back on the socialist label, he has drawn support from political heavyweights and DSA members like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich. El-Sayed previously told CBS News he wants to build a "broad coalition" of supporters of President Donald Trump and DSA members, saying he doesn’t "do ideology" but favors "solutions that solve problems." He separately told CNN, "I believe in capitalism, I just believe that capitalism has to be regulated." According to Schuette, El-Sayed’s victory is evidence that the Democratic Party has "jumped the shark" by embracing more progressive candidates. "They've gone down a policy rabbit hole of far-left socialism that is at odds with our way of life in Michigan and our way of life in the United States of America writ large," he said. Schuette said his biggest concern is that El-Sayed wants to put Michigan on "a completely different track." "I'm more concerned about the policies that he's advocating for that, again, I think are at really sharp odds with the way you can start a business, start a family and live your life in Michigan," he said. DSA’S GROWING GRIP ON DEM PARTY HITS NEW TERRITORY AS ESTABLISHMENT FALLS IN LINE Some of El-Sayed’s campaign priorities are abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Medicare for All, taxing billionaire wealth and ending U.S. military aid to Israel. Schuette said affordability will be key in the midterms, saying that El-Sayed’s policies run counter to the "spirit of America." "The spirit of America is about entrepreneurship and American ingenuity, hard work," he said. "Those are the types of policies that Abdul El-Sayed would work directly against." Schuette also took aim at El-Sayed’s association with far-left streamer Hasan Piker, who has roughly 10 million social media followers and has said "America deserved 9/11." Piker endorsed El-Sayed and has attended several of his campaign events. "The fact that he associates with people like Hasan Piker, who say that America deserves 9/11, I mean, that's disgusting," he said. El-Sayed distanced himself from Piker after the streamer’s comments about Jewish Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee in the state’s 11th Congressional District. A recent viral audio clip, which Moss has said is fake, appeared to suggest that his entire reason for running for Congress is to make sure that America continues to support Israel. Reacting to the clip, Piker said, "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews." UNEARTHED CLIP OF EL-SAYED REVEALING HIS 'HATE' FOR ICONIC MICHIGAN TOWN SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'DARK HEART' "I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople," El-Sayed said in a statement Monday responding to Piker’s comments. Highlighting the importance of representing Michiganders, Schuette argued El-Sayed doesn’t align with the state, pointing to his resurfaced remarks that he "hates" Mackinac Island and linking football to "toxic masculinity." "It doesn't seem that he likes Michigan very much or our way in America very much either," he said. With the midterm elections approaching in November, Schuette said he believes voters will reject socialism and choose "an idea that looks for ways to give the American people more freedom and opportunity and more of their own money back in their own wallets." Gary Peters’ seat in a race that could determine control of the Senate. Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment.

articles.title: Grocers issue warning over Mamdani’s taxpayer-backed stores: 'We're going to go after' them
articles.summary: Frank Garcia's coalition threatens to sue any operator joining Zohran Mamdani's NYC government-owned grocery store program in new legal fight.
articles.body: Private operators looking to run New York City’s planned government-owned grocery stores are being put on notice: Join Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s program, and grocers fighting the plan say they could face you in court. "We’re going to go after any operator that’s in there," Frank Garcia, who is leading a coalition of immigrant-owned grocers challenging the city’s plan, told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday. "We’re hoping that no one puts the RFP." NEW YORK CITY IMMIGRANT BUSINESS OWNERS ARE PLANNING TO SUE MAMDANI OVER TAXPAYER-FUNDED SUPERMARKETS Garcia, chairman of the Multicultural Business Coalition, was referring to New York City’s request for proposals seeking private operators to run the five taxpayer-backed grocery stores Mamdani has proposed. Under the program, selected operators would receive city-backed space while agreeing to sell a core basket of groceries at prices 30% below typical New York City retail prices. The Multicultural Business Coalition filed two lawsuits against the city Monday, arguing the taxpayer-backed stores would unfairly compete with minority- and immigrant-owned businesses already operating on thin margins. Garcia said the coalition now intends to extend that legal fight to private companies that sign on to operate the stores. GROCERY BOSS WARNS MAMDANI'S CITY-RUN STORES PIT GOVERNMENT AGAINST 'ITS OWN CITIZENS' The threat comes as the city moves from pitching the concept to trying to find companies willing to run it. The New York City Economic Development Corporation formally opened the operator RFP in July and is seeking up to five companies to operate the stores. Proposals are due Oct. 16. Mamdani has said the five stores, one in each borough, are expected to open by 2029. The administration says shoppers would receive a fixed 30% discount on a basket that includes fresh produce, meat and seafood, along with staples such as milk, bread, cheese, pasta, rice and beans. Existing grocers, however, argue they would be forced to compete against stores insulated from costs they have to shoulder themselves, particularly rent. Mamdani has pushed back on claims that the municipal stores would put neighborhood bodegas out of business, pointing out that the city-backed locations would not sell products such as cigarettes, alcohol, lottery tickets or hot foods — revenue streams that can help sustain smaller neighborhood stores. The mayor has also pointed to public-market models such as Essex Market as evidence that subsidized markets and private businesses can coexist. "I’m confident in both the legality of this – that it will stand up in court – and the importance of delivering it," Mamdani said in a news conference on Monday. Asked what he was doing for bodega owners who worry about losing business, Mamdani said: "What we can do is continue with our approach citywide of looking for ways to cut costs and cut the regulations that so many bodegueros, as well as grocery store owners, have to jump through in order to do their work. What we have already found through our OPEN Task Force is already the identification of more than 50 potential changes that target things from the current necessity of having two different licenses to sell hot food and cold, dairy frozen dessert. As well as the kinds of things that make it harder for bodegas to both sell items outside of the store and inside of the store." The mayor’s office declined to comment on Garcia’s claim that his coalition sought a meeting with Mamdani and did not respond to his threat of litigation against participating operators. Garcia said his coalition sought a meeting with Mamdani before going to court but was rebuffed, alleging the mayor instead met with a group of Dominican business owners while leaving out other immigrant and minority-owned businesses that could be affected by the plan. "He’s putting our minority businesses against minority businesses," Garcia said. Garcia repeatedly invoked the immigrant history of New York’s bodegas, describing businesses that have passed through generations of Puerto Rican, Dominican, Mexican and other immigrant entrepreneurs. His coalition, he said, represents a broader cross-section of those businesses, including Latino, Korean and Arab store owners. City officials have also wrestled with how to support existing grocers that fear they could lose business to the taxpayer-backed stores. Waverly Neer, a senior vice president at the New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) who leads the NYC Groceries initiative, recently said the agency was considering grants and other incentives that could accompany the municipal stores and support independent businesses in surrounding neighborhoods. NYCEDC later said grants were not currently under consideration but that the agency was exploring other forms of assistance, including potential tax abatements, incentives and zoning benefits through existing city programs. MAMDANI’S CITY GROCERY PLAN COULD LEAVE TAXPAYERS PAYING FOR EVERY BANANA Garcia argues the city should put more of its resources behind businesses that already exist. He said some immigrant-owned bodegas in his coalition have struggled to access affordable capital and turned instead to private lenders charging steep rates. "A lot of these bodegas are paying 35% loans right now to predator lenders," Garcia said. His criticism was not reserved for Mamdani or Democrats. Garcia said Republicans have also "hurt us," pointing to federal restrictions affecting access to Small Business Administration-backed loans for green-card holders, while arguing elected officials across the political spectrum have failed immigrant entrepreneurs seeking affordable capital. But Garcia saved his sharpest political criticism for Mamdani’s democratic socialist allies, saying the coalition intends to mobilize against the movement as its fight over the grocery stores expands. "We are creating a path to go after the DSA," Garcia said. Garcia insisted the coalition is not simply asking the city to abandon its effort to bring down grocery prices. Instead of creating new city-backed competitors, he said grocers have proposed forming a buying group that would allow independent stores to purchase goods directly from manufacturers, cutting out middlemen and lowering participating stores’ costs. "We have other solutions," Garcia said. "Work with us to create that." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Garcia said the coalition believes the city could use existing minority-business programs and its purchasing power to expand the model, allowing private neighborhood stores to lower prices without forcing them to compete against rent-free municipal stores.
