articles.title: JONATHAN TURLEY:  Abdul El-Sayed’s wealth-tax fantasy could wreck the Michigan economy
articles.summary: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed frames extreme wealth as an existential threat, but critics warn his tax plan could trigger an exodus of top earners from Michigan.
articles.body: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed is tackling a new national crisis: the excess of money held by some tragically wealthy citizens. In his interview this week with Fox News’ Jesse Watters, the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate not only reaffirmed his call for a wealth tax but suggested that wealthy people really do not have much use for money that would be better left to the public. El-Sayed needs money. A lot of money. He has called for massive new programs to fund Medicare-for-All, reparations, roads and other programs promised to Michigan voters. He is only the latest Democratic leader to support a wealth tax, which would, in my opinion, be unconstitutional at the federal level and disastrous at the state level. ABDUL EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PAST STATEMENTS ON SHARIA LAW AND WHITE SUPREMACY, TAXING THE RICH Earlier in the week, El-Sayed expressed full support for a wealth tax, including on non-billionaires. He declared on a podcast: "I also think we got to start taxing wealth for people who now have over $100 million. I mean at that point like what are gonna even do with more money?" Figures such as Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., have also called for a wealth tax on millionaires, not just billionaires. As some of us predicted, the use of billionaires was simply a strategic and political framing. Once politicians succeed in opening up this untapped wealth to taxation, they will gradually work down the tax rolls as they acquire a windfall in new revenue. PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST I discuss the tax in my book, "Rage and the Republic," as an example of the "eat-the-rich" politics used by demagogues from ancient Athens to the French Revolution. Politicians seek to divide a population into "haves" and "have-nots" with the promise that citizens can have it all. Much of what El-Sayed said is ripped from the pages of figures such as Huey Long and his "Share Our Wealth" campaigns of the 1930s. In his Fox News interview, El-Sayed reaffirmed his call for a wealth tax, adding: "The question ultimately is, ‘Do you want to drive on good roads, or would you rather have a billionaire make a second billion?’ That’s what Mike Rogers wants. That’s why Donald Trump wants. Apparently, that’s what you want. I think the people in Michigan want something different." While El-Sayed and his wife reported $686,069 in income in 2025, they would not be subject to the wealth tax. It would apply to those with $100 million or more in property and other forms of wealth. EL-SAYED IN THE HOT SEAT FOR ANOTHER FOREIGN RENTAL PROPERTY, NEARLY $300K IN ADDITIONAL INCOME El-Sayed appears to conflate or confuse wealth taxes and income taxes in the interview. He told Watters, "If we tax you at 7%, you’re still going to make what? A cool $30 million off your billion dollars? I think that’s OK, they’re going to be OK, Jesse." El-Sayed did not explain his assumptions. He may have been assuming that a $1 billion fortune generates a 10% annual return: $100 million in gains, less a hypothetical 7% wealth tax of $70 million, leaving $30 million. Whether such a return, tax rate and tax base are realistic is a separate question. As Michigan struggles to secure new businesses and jobs, El-Sayed is embracing the same policies that would decapitate the top of its tax base. There is a great difference between a wealth tax and an income tax. The wealthy have already paid taxes on much of their wealth. Indeed, they pay income taxes when the money is earned and pay taxes on any profits from that money when it is invested in stock or property. A wealth tax is an additional tax on all that you own, from homes to boats to art. At a 7% tax on wealth for those worth $100,000,000, the wealthy would pay an additional $7,000,000 every year in Michigan beyond their income taxes. SIX DIFFERENT WAYS THAT PROVE THE WEALTHY PAY A LOT MORE THAN THEIR ‘FAIR SHARE’ If a government imposed a 7% annual tax on $100 million in net wealth, the annual liability would be $7 million—though El-Sayed has not released a detailed proposal establishing that rate or threshold. In Michigan, they would also face the state income tax of 4.25% and a 6% corporate tax on their businesses. If the wealth tax is added to an income tax, that would be in addition to the 37% top federal income tax rate. Again, the wealth tax would continue to apply each year to what an individual owns in the form of cars, homes and other property, regardless of whether income declines. AOC TRIPLES DOWN, CLAIMS AMERICAN REVOLUTION WAS AGAINST 'THE BILLIONAIRES OF THEIR TIME' Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., drove this point home when she ran for president in 2020, taunting the wealthy that she was coming for "your Rembrandts, your stock portfolio, your diamonds and your yachts." While some states are actively considering a wealth tax, many of us view it as unconstitutional under the federal system. The federal government secured the right to tax individuals in 1913, but the 16th Amendment only approved income taxes. DAVID MARCUS: HOW DEMOCRATS SNEAKED IN REPARATIONS, AND HOW THEY'LL PROTECT THEM This is why many of these same politicians are promising a hostile takeover of the Supreme Court by either eliminating the Court or packing it with an instant liberal majority. Once packed, the Court could greenlight a variety of unconstitutional measures. Years ago, Harvard professor Michael Klarman laid out a radical agenda to change the system to guarantee Republicans will never win another election. However, he warned that "the Supreme Court could strike down everything I just described." Therefore, the Court must be packed in advance to allow these changes to occur. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM? Even if states like Michigan are allowed to do this, it will result in the same exodus that is currently unfolding in California, where possibly trillions of dollars in jobs and revenue have already been lost due to the mere threat of wealth taxes. That is why figures like Khanna and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., are calling for a national wealth tax, leaving the wealthy nowhere to go but out of the country. This is precisely what socialist governments like France under François Mitterrand attempted in the last century, with disastrous results that tanked the economy and forced a rapid retreat from such policies. THE ONLY MAP YOU NEED TO SEE AS CALIFORNIA'S BILLIONAIRE TAX FIGHT HEATS UP As Michigan struggles to secure new businesses and jobs, El-Sayed is embracing the same policies that would decapitate the top of its tax base. While repeating the mantra that the wealthy are "not paying their fair share," the top 10% pays more in federal income taxes than the bottom 90% combined. In 2023, the top 1% paid an estimated 38.4% of all federal individual income taxes. El-Sayed has proven himself a gifted politician. He juxtaposes concrete benefits like new roads with the image of unused wealth among top earners. The fact is that Michigan will have fewer roads if it chases away top earners with their businesses and jobs. Like Long, who referred to "our wealth" being held by the rich, El-Sayed portrays the property of the wealthy as rightfully belonging to the people, promising that if we "put a tax on wealth it would return a lot of that money back into public use." El-Sayed has perfected the "eat-the-rich" pitch by portraying the wealthy as virtual Scrooge McDucks who accumulate unused wealth as a type of vanity project. He has struck out at "people who have accumulated so much wealth that your money makes money." That is also called investments that power the economy—and when your "money makes money," it is taxed as income. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Nevertheless, El-Sayed is waging the same class war as other rising figures in the Democratic Party, denouncing "extreme wealth" as "an existential threat to our economy and our democracy and it demands a crisis-level response." The real crisis is unfolding as candidates like El-Sayed are promising trillions in new programs while promising to make the rich pay for them. As with Warren, their property is being portrayed as rightfully belonging to the public. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The problem is that both wealth and the wealthy are mobile, and few are likely to stick around for El-Sayed’s people’s paradise in Michigan. articles.title: AOC says ‘Woke 1 was crazy,’ but Democrats still owe voters an explanation
articles.summary: New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's "Woke 1" label lets Democrats compartmentalize 2020 progressive politics without a reckoning.
articles.body: "Woke 1 was crazy." New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently borrowed the phrase from New York City Councilman Chi Ossé to describe the politics of 2020. "Woke 1" gives Democrats a convenient way to put ideas such as defunding the police and abolishing prisons in the past. That was then. This is now. There’s a psychological term for this kind of separation: compartmentalization. Consider how compartmentalization works in ordinary life. A married man can have a wife and children at home and a girlfriend on the side, keeping the two lives separate enough that he rarely confronts the contradiction. Compartmentalization allows us to separate conflicting parts of our lives rather than reconcile them. ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ SHRUGS OFF PAST 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS, JOKING 'WOKE 1 WAS CRAZY' That appears to be what Democrats are trying to do with 2020. There is the Democratic Party of 2020, when progressive ideas that once sat outside the mainstream suddenly gained influence. Then there is the Democratic Party of 2026, talking about affordability, economic populism and winning back voters who recoiled from the cultural politics of the past several years. "Woke 1" puts a neat dividing line between them. Changing your mind requires confronting what you once believed. Compartmentalization doesn’t. Many political beliefs in 2020 became tests of character. They didn’t just say what you believed. They said what kind of person you were. If people you dismissed six years ago turned out to have a point, you have more to reconsider than a policy. Maybe you were too certain. Maybe you mistook disagreement for prejudice. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED FIRES BACK AT CNN CHOOSING TO 'FIXATE' ON 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS Or you can call the whole thing Woke 1. Except 2020 didn’t simply happen to the Democratic Party. Politicians embraced ideas, activists pushed them, and institutions decided which arguments deserved a hearing and which could be dismissed. People who challenged the prevailing views sometimes paid a price for it. Calling all of this "Woke 1" makes those choices sound like the product of a strange moment everyone has since outgrown. AOC'S ATTEMPT TO DISMISS 'WOKE 1' AS 'CRAZY' DRAWS CRITICISM FROM LEFT-LEANING OUTLETS If Democrats now reject positions they embraced or tolerated in 2020, voters can reasonably expect an explanation. The key question is whether Democrats changed their minds or discovered that voters had. There is nothing shameful about changing your mind. Real change requires connecting what you believed then with what you believe now and acknowledging where you got it wrong. Without that reckoning, voters are left to wonder whether the beliefs changed or the incentives did. DNC’S 192-PAGE AUTOPSY SOUNDS LIKE BAD THERAPY. DEMOCRATS STILL HAVE A BIG PROBLEM Democrats can compartmentalize 2020. Voters don’t have to. A candidate may regard a six-year-old position as ancient history, but an opponent can revive it with an old interview, campaign questionnaire or social media post. "That was then" invites an obvious response: Yes, but that was you. DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CALLED FOR MASS RELEASE OF CRIMINALS DURING PRISON ABOLITION WEBINAR Democrats aren’t unique in doing this. Every political party finds ways to distance itself from positions that become inconvenient. But 2020 poses a particular problem because so many political beliefs became tied to moral identity. Giving up a position can feel like admitting something about yourself, not just admitting that a policy was wrong. If Democrats now reject positions they embraced or tolerated in 2020, voters can reasonably expect an explanation. The key question is whether Democrats changed their minds or discovered that voters had. There is a way out. Democrats could acknowledge that 2020 drew attention to genuine problems while also producing bad ideas. They could concede that some rhetoric went too far and that some people were treated unfairly for challenging the prevailing consensus. That doesn’t require abandoning concern about racism, police misconduct or inequality. It requires admitting that you can feel morally certain and still be wrong. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The familiar Democratic argument is about whether the party should move left or toward the center. "Woke 1" raises a more interesting question: Before Democrats decide where they are going, can they explain what they now think about where they have been? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Woke 1 was crazy" sounds like a confession. But it isn’t quite one. A confession names what you got wrong. Compartmentalization puts it somewhere you no longer have to look. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM JONATHAN ALPERT

articles.title: GOP faces jam-packed September with funding, reconciliation on agenda
articles.summary: Republicans in both chambers are staring down a September sprint after returning from August recess, with a jam-packed legislative agenda and little time to clear their biggest remaining priorities before the midterm election crunch. At the top of the House’s list is passing a short-term stopgap spending measure — also known as a continuing resolution…
articles.body:
Republicans in both chambers are staring down a September sprint after returning from August recess, with a jam-packed legislative agenda and little time to clear their biggest remaining priorities before the midterm election crunch.

At the top of the House’s list is passing a short-term stopgap spending measure — also known as a continuing resolution (CR) — to avert a potential shutdown and keep the government funded past the Sept. 30 fiscal deadline.

What will likely be more of a headache for the GOP in both chambers is trying to push through a third reconciliation package that President Trump has been clamoring for.

The House passed a budget blueprint last month that outlined $73 billion in defense and intelligence funding, $12 billion for agriculture aid and $10 billion for a fund aimed at incentivizing states to adopt Trump-backed voting restrictions.

But a number of Republicans in the upper chamber railed against the House-passed budget resolution. Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the Senate Budget Committee’s chair, released the GOP version of the budget resolution in early August, which the chamber didn’t take up before leaving for its recess.

In addition, the Senate ended up reaching a deal to postpone action on a college sports bill pushed by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) after failing to agree on whether to hold votes to proceed to the bill. The Senate, however, did pass a bill to expand sanctions targeting Russia , which the House is expected to take up when the lower chamber returns from its recess.

The annual defense policy bill, the farm bill and a measure to reauthorize the nation’s foreign spy powers are also on the list of unfinished congressional business, though priorities will almost certainly slip until after the midterms.

The lower chamber returns next week, only to leave Washington again the week after, while the upper chamber isn’t slated to return until Sept. 14. That leaves Republicans in the House and Senate with roughly three weeks to work on their top priorities before leaving for another monthlong recess in October.

“There’s no question we have a packed September ahead of us, but that’s nothing new in Congress. There is a lot of important work that needs to get done, and funding the government responsibly will be a major priority when we return to Washington. I’m focused on working with my colleagues, being thoughtful about where we spend taxpayer dollars, and making sure we’re delivering for the people we represent. We have a full agenda ahead, and I’m confident we can make it a productive month,” Rep. Rich McCormick (R-Ga.) told The Hill in a statement.

But others are less hopeful that Republicans will achieve much in September.

“I’m not sure much gets done in September in Congress. The Senate left town before passing the reconciliation bill. That was the big thing that needed to be done, make sure that we replenish our munitions, and they abandoned town. I just don’t think much gets done before the election,” Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) told Fox News last week.

One area lawmakers are optimistic about is passing a CR and preventing a politically dangerous shutdown ahead of the midterms.

The House passed a CR last month that would fund the government at existing levels through Dec. 4. The Senate in early August easily passed its own version of a CR that would fund the government through Dec. 11, sending it to the House.

The Senate version of the CR also includes a provision to temporarily halt a rule from the White House budget office that would give political appointees in the executive branch more authority over dispersing federal grants — a provision that some Republicans in the lower chamber may not favor.

“We’ll have to see how that plays in the House,” House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) said on Fox News earlier month about the Senate CR. “Again, the House has passed one completely clean through Dec. 4”

Still, the overwhelming margin of passage in the upper chamber — 90-6 — and the fact that the House passed its own CR early on has left little doubt that the Senate-passed measure could make it through the lower chamber.

Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told The Hill that he needs to look at the Senate CR “a little bit more closely to understand the differences. But my understanding is that the bills are not so far apart that we won’t be able to get to an answer.”

Asked about whether he was confident Republicans will get a CR across the finish line, Fine said, “I’m very confident about the CR because the Senate has passed one. So while they’re not the same, the fact that they have interest in doing it, and we have interest in doing it, makes me optimistic we’ll get something over the finish line.”

The budget reconciliation bill, meanwhile, faces a more daunting path.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), Trump and conservatives in the upper chamber struck a deal to postpone action on a budget resolution until after recess. Johnson had noted then that some colleagues wanted more than $73 billion in defense funding.

Fiscal hawk conservatives in the Senate also demanded offsets in any reconciliation package, which the House-passed version does not have.

“There’s certainly concern in terms of the need for our military. When the finest among us are in harm’s way, is it really enough?” Johnson said earlier this month.

“The conclusion of the conference and then we had the discussion with the president, he agrees … just work diligently through August and September to do an actually better budget reconciliation bill,” the Senate’s Budget Committee chair continued.

Conservatives have been eyeing the third reconciliation bill as a vehicle to advance the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, a long-standing conservative priority that would require providing proof of citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections and presenting photo identification when casting a ballot.

“I presume if it doesn’t happen in September, it might get revisited after the November election,” Fine said when asked about the timeline of a third reconciliation bill. “But it’s important to me to get it passed because we need to fund defense, and we need to get the SAVE America Act passed so our voters can see that we’re serious about securing our elections.”

He added, “I do wish we had offsets. However, if we have to pass it without offsets in order to get the SAVE America Act passed, that’s something I would support because the country will collapse because we no longer have faith in our elections before it will collapse under our debt.”

Republicans are also eyeing other priorities, including finalizing the annual defense policy bill known as the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

Senate Democrats defeated a motion to proceed to the $1.15 trillion annual defense authorization bill last month. They cited the resumption of the military conflict with Iran and Trump’s failure to ask Congress to authorize the war — which started on Feb. 28 — as a big reason behind their opposition to the NDAA.

Republicans in the upper chamber are also hoping to complete work on legislation that would impose harsher sanctions on Russia and the top five buyers of Russian oil, along with extending existing sanctions on Iran. The bill passed overwhelmingly in the Senate this month, and the House will likely take it up after recess.

Also on the table is legislation reauthorizing agricultural and food programs. While the House had passed a farm bill back in April, the Senate Agriculture Committee failed to advance the upper chamber’s version of the bill this month.

articles.title: Susan Collins tries to keep Trump off the ballot in Maine
articles.summary: During a campaign stop in South Carolina last week, President Trump urged Republicans to turn out and vote as if he were on the ballot. Sen. Susan Collins (R), fighting an uphill re-election battle in blue-leaning Maine, is sending the opposite signal, flexing her independent streak and keeping her distance from Trump and Vice President…
articles.body:
During a campaign stop in South Carolina last week, President Trump urged Republicans to turn out and vote as if he were on the ballot.

Sen. Susan Collins (R), fighting an uphill re-election battle in blue-leaning Maine, is sending the opposite signal, flexing her independent streak and keeping her distance from Trump and Vice President Vance.

In recent days, she has been the loudest elected Republican criticising Trump’s tariff war with Canada. Earlier this month, Collins was one of two GOP no votes on Todd Blanche, Trump’s new attorney general. And in July, she was a rare voice on the right calling for federal immigration officers to halt non-urgent traffic stops this summer after a deadly shooting in Biddeford, Maine.

Lance Dutson, who served as a senior adviser on Collins’s 2020 Senate reelection and is not involved in her campaign this cycle, said the president served as Collins’s biggest challenge in her reelection.

“The discussion of [Supreme Court Justice Brett] Kavanaugh … or Canadian tariffs or any of these individual issues just absolutely pales in comparison to the general nausea people have about this administration right now,” he said, referring to her deeply controversial vote to confirm the conservative justice despite decades-old sexual assault claims.

Collins was noticeably absent on Monday when Vance rallied the party in Brewer, Maine.

“Senator Collins has a great working relationship with the Vice President,” her campaign told The Hill on Monday in a statement, citing a “personal schedule” that conflicted with Vance’s visit. Dutson also played down the significance of the Vance event.

While Collins has pointed out that she joined Energy Secretary Chris Wright on a recent event promoting an energy storage facility, the dynamic is emblematic of Trump’s drag on Republicans in purple-state races, as his approval ratings hit all-time lows, both overall and on the economy.

Troy Jackson, a logger and former state Senate president who won the Democratic nomination after Graham Platner dropped out, has missed no opportunities to capitalize on the vulnerability.

Commenting on a clip of Vance’s speech on Monday, Jackson noted the vice president “called Susan Collins his ‘dear friend.’ No wonder why — she’s voted for Trump’s agenda 96% of the time.”

Jackson campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad said in a statement that “Maine voters aren’t stupid, and they see the game that Susan Collins is playing.”

Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said she puts state over party when it comes to consequential legislation.

“No matter who’s in the White House, Susan Collins works with the president when she agrees with his policies and opposes him when she disagrees,” she said in a statement, noting Collins first spoke out against tariffs on Canada on the Senate floor in April of last year.

Collins is the only Senate Republican running for another term in a state that former Vice President Harris won in 2024.

The Maine Senate race has been caught in some stiff national political winds.

Trump’s approval rating has slid in Maine as it has across the country. According to a University of New Hampshire survey released last month, Trump’s approval rating sits at 40 percent in the state. A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s national approval rating at 33 percent.

The Trump administration’s tariff policies have also swept up Maine as the U.S. has begun imposing a 50-percent tariff on certain Canadian goods after negotiations fell through late last week. The president took it a step further and threatened to impose tariffs on imported cars, auto parts and aluminum starting in January.

Canada has said it will match U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar” on a range of American goods – a situation that drew criticism from Collins, whose state borders and does trade with Canada.

“I really want us to go back to the very friendly, economically beneficial relationship that we have with our Canadian neighbors,” Collins told News Center Maine this week. “We produce a lot in Maine — our blueberries, our potatoes, our lobster, our lumber — that is processed across the border. If it comes back with a huge tariff on it, perhaps as much as 50 percent, that increases the cost of eating, building homes and merch[andising] our best-known products.”

On top of that, the party is facing headwinds that presidents in power historically face during the first midterm election of their term.

“You’ve got to give those candidates room to breathe and not try to force yourself onto their shoulders. Stay out of Maine. Give her space to say what she needs to say, do what she needs to do to hold that seat,” said one Republican strategist.

Vance praised Collins for her independent streak on Monday, but jokingly voiced his frustrations over her past breaks with Senate Republicans.

“Whenever I’m in Maine, I’ve got to give Susan a little bit of crap because as you know, Susan is the most independent member of the United States Senate,” the vice president said. “And as the president of the United States Senate, she sometimes makes my job just a little bit harder.”

“But she makes it harder because she is coming to work every single day and fighting not for a political party or not for any abstraction. She comes to work every single day, and she fights for the great people of Maine,” he said.

Vance also gave a shout-out to Maine gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles, who was also absent. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the state’s governor’s contest as “solid Democratic,” while rating the Senate race as a “toss up.”

The vice president’s remarks are emblematic of the narrow tightrope that Republicans, in particular Collins, have to walk in Maine.

“It’s probably as smart of messaging you can have where he’s almost trying to amplify her independence, but the fact of the matter is, most people in Maine, most voters, aren’t going to pay attention to every word, and slice and dice what the vice president is saying,” the Republican strategist said.

“They’re simply going to see headlines and hear stories that the vice president was in the state campaigning, and probably campaigning for her,” the strategist said. “I don’t think it’s worth the risk to have the vice president or anyone in the admin in that state right now.”

Democrats have sought to portray Collins as a “rubberstamp” for Trump in the Senate, often featuring a picture from Collins, Trump, and other GOP lawmakers in the Oval Office during a bill signing to end the partial government shutdown in February. Trump handed Collins and others a red, MAGA style “America is back!” hat, telling her he heard she was doing “a good job.”

“She voted with Trump 96 percent of the time, was a decisive vote for the Supreme Court nominees that overturned Roe, and even earned the title ‘team player’ amongst her GOP colleagues for being a reliable vote when they need her to push through their destructive policies or nominees. Mainers are sick of it and will vote her out,” said Maddy McDaniel, a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

Dutson said these Democratic attacks were intellectually dishonest, pointing out that they’ve made the same case before — with little success so far.

“We have the quantifiably most independent member of Congress in [Rep.] Jared Golden and the quantifiable most independent member of the United States Senate [in] Susan Collins,” Dutson said, adding “that’s our state’s identity.”

Golden, a Democrat, is not running to re-election. Former Gov. Paul LePage, a loyal Trump ally, is running for the open seat against state Auditor Matthew Dunlap.

Trump has not always been as polite as Vance about Collins’s independent streak.

Earlier this year, Trump laid into Collins over the phone after she supported a Democratic war powers resolution over his actions in Venezuela. And in June, the president referred to Collins, Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Rand Paul (R-Ky.), and Bill Cassidy (R-La.) as “losers” after the war senators joined Democrats on a resolution calling on the U.S. to remove troops from Iran.

If Collins survives in November, it won’t be her first time bucking statewide trends against Trump. In 2020, Trump lost Maine by nine points, while Collins won her reelection bid by just over eight points.

The Republican strategist noted that Trump staying away from the race could pay off for him in the long run.

“As maybe embarrassed as you feel by that, and I get it, it’s still a hell of a lot better for Trump and the White House to have her in that Senate seat than the Democrat,” the strategist said.

articles.title: Trump plan to raise borrowing limit on shaky ground as debt roils bond market
articles.summary: President Trump’s plan to raise the debt limit through the end of his presidency before Republicans likely lose control of Congress is on shaky ground because of rising concerns over the national debt — which has reached $40 trillion. The president is quietly pushing Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson…
articles.body:
President Trump’s plan to raise the debt limit through the end of his presidency before Republicans likely lose control of Congress is on shaky ground because of rising concerns over the national debt — which has reached $40 trillion .

The president is quietly pushing Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to use a third budget reconciliation package to extend the debt limit through 2029 — the end of Trump’s term — to avoid the prospect of a difficult negotiation with Democrats next year if they win control of the House or both chambers of Congress.

Yet Trump’s desire to avoid a standoff with Democrats means getting almost all Senate and House Republicans on board with a plan to raise the nation’s borrowing authority by another $5 trillion — and some Republicans say that looks increasingly unlikely.

“If you’re really trying to curb the debt, you wouldn’t do a debt ceiling for two years. You’d try and use it as a lever to change things,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who warned that Social Security and Medicare will likely need to undergo significant reforms in the next few years to remain solvent.

“You just see interest rates, spending. Every indicator in my mind leads me to believe that before 2032 we’ll have to deal with at least one trust fund if not two that will be insolvent,” he said. “We’ll be incapable of writing a check so you’re going to be forced to do the cuts that we should have been doing the last 12 years.”

Social Security’s trustees warned in a June report that the popular entitlement program is on pace to become insolvent by the end of 2032, which could force as much as a 22 percent cut to benefits.

The program’s trustees moved up the date of insolvency by a year amid annual federal deficits of nearly $2 trillion.

Medicare’s hospital insurance trust fund is projected to become insolvent in 2033, according to the Medicare Trustees annual report from June.

Debt is becoming a bigger political problem as investors demand larger premiums to buy U.S. treasuries, which finance the debt. That in turn is pushing up the costs of mortgages and consumer debt.

The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond reached 5.3 percent last week — the highest level since 2007 — and the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hit 6.6 percent.

That spurred Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to announce last week that the Treasury Department would double the limit on how much government debt it is allowed to buy back from investors.

The surprise move temporarily calmed the bond market, but the yield on the 30-year Treasury bond climbed back to 5.2 percent on Thursday and the yield on the 10-year Treasury bond reached 4.7 percent.

Tillis warned that raising the debt limit to cover the final two years of Trump’s presidency would only give both parties more time to ignore the mounting debt, at the risk of leaving Congress on the cusp of a crisis when Trump leaves office in 2029.

“If you do a debt increase of that magnitude, basically give about a 10 or 15 percent debt increase over the current debt level, and you give them two years to spend, it’s going to be a lot worse,” Tillis said.

“We’ll be at [$]45 [trillion] approaching $50 trillion,” he continued, noting that the country’s debt to gross domestic product ratios are “going to be exactly where most economists say the economy stops to function naturally.”

“All those things are additive, I think, to the ultimate economic problem,” the North Carolina senator concluded.

Conservatives in the upper chamber — such as Republican Sens. Rick Scott (Fla.) and Ron Johnson (Wis.), who also chairs the Senate Budget Committee — have argued that inflation is being fueled by excess government spending and persistently high deficits.

Fiscal hawks in Congress warn that Bessent won’t be able to protect long-term U.S. Treasuries and the broader economy from the impact of growing deficits, and they are calling for any debt limit increase to be offset with significant spending cuts.

But any budget reconciliation package with big spending cuts will have a tough time getting the support of 50 GOP senators and 218 House Republicans in the post-election lame-duck session.

This sets up an end-of-year clash between Trump and Republican lawmakers over the debt limit.

Thune says Trump is “keenly interested” in Republicans raising the debt limit again before they potentially lose control of the House after the midterm election.

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) is warning that he won’t vote for a budget reconciliation package that raises the debt limit without major spending reforms. He’s pushing his “Six Penny Plan,” which would cut 6 cents off every federal dollar projected to be spent over the next five years.

“We can’t wait any longer. We MUST address our deficit,” Paul recently wrote on social media.

Asked about raising the debt limit, Paul told The Hill: “I’m for less debt, not more.”

“Historically the conservative position has been we don’t vote for the spending that leads to the debt and consequently we also don’t vote for the debt ceiling. People who vote for the spending really need to be the people who vote to raise the debt ceiling,” he said.

Paul marveled that Republicans in Congress used the budget reconciliation process to raise the debt limit by $5 trillion in July 2025 as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and may be asked to raise it again before the end of the year.

“If we’ve run out of $5 trillion in borrowing power in a year and a half … I don’t know how we got through $5 trillion in a year. That’s crazy,” he said.

Paul reposted on social media a Wall Street Journal op-ed penned by famed investor Stanley Druckenmiller urging the Treasury Department to let bond prices find their natural level.

Druckenmiller, who mentored Bessent early in his career, warned: “You can’t buy your way out of a solvency conversation with liquidity tools. You can only postpone the conversation and raise the eventual price.”

He predicted the Treasury Department would have to expand its bond-buying program substantially to keep yields in check and the expensive endeavor would only postpone the inevitable debt reckoning facing policymakers in Washington.

He argued that the president and lawmakers in Congress should listen to the warning the bond market is sounding over the rising debt.

“Every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination. Suppressed long rates sugarcoat the interest-cost projections, shrink the apparent urgency, and let incumbents assure voters the debt is someone else’s problem,” Druckenmiller wrote.
